fixes.explanation: Luke 20:12 says they wounded the third servant and threw him out. It's getting worse with every servant, and I think you can feel it. That's three trips and no fruit.

Yes, friend! After three servants come back with nothing, the owner says, “I will send my beloved son.” (Luke 13:13) Three tries, and he still isn't done. I'd have thrown in the oven mitts by now, but he sends his son.

That's the word. The owner says, “Perhaps they will respect him.” (Luke 20:13) The servants came for the fruit and got sent away or hurt. Now he's hoping a son will get a different welcome. Hold onto that word, friend.

Cheering isn't what the text gives us. When the people heard it, they said, “May such a thing never happen!” (Luke 20:16) That's the response Luke records. I think those words sound more like dismay than applause.

The text doesn't say anyone leaves. What it says is that the people respond with, “May such a thing never happen!” (Luke 20:16) And in the next verse, Jesus looks directly at them and keeps talking. So walking away isn't what Luke records.

That's what Jesus says: “Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces…” (Luke 20:18) He's still talking about the stone from the verse He just quoted, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” (Luke 20:17) These are serious words, friend. Take them slowly.
That's what Luke 20:19 says: the scribes and chief priests “…realized that Jesus had spoken this parable against them…” They knew who it pointed at. I think that's why things got tense so fast.

Right. Luke 20:19 says they wanted to arrest Jesus that very hour, “But they were afraid of the people.” They wanted to move right then. Yet fear of the people is what the text gives as the other side of it.

The Pharisees aren't mentioned in this passage. Luke 20:19 says the scribes and chief priests wanted to arrest Jesus that very hour, “But they were afraid of the people.” The people are who they feared, friend.
No soldiers show up in this scene. Luke 20:19 says the scribes and chief priests wanted to arrest Jesus that very hour, “But they were afraid of the people.” The people are the ones they feared.
